H1.text: A tailor measures in inches. A road sign shows kilometres per hour. Your physics book wants metres per second.

H2.text: Same world, different units. So we must switch between them, without mistakes.

H3.text: Aarav's bicycle meter reads eighteen kilometres per hour.

H4.text: His homework asks for the speed in metres per second. Is it still eighteen?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will convert it in one line, and never get it backwards.

P1.text: So what does converting a unit really mean?

P2.text: The quantity stays the same. Only the unit changes, so the number changes too.

P3.text: Remember the rule from episode one. n one u one equals n two u two.

P4.text: To convert, we use a conversion factor. It is a fraction that is exactly equal to one.

P5.text: One kilometre over one thousand metres is one. The top and the bottom are the same length.

P6.text: Multiplying by one never changes a quantity.

S1.text: Let's ride with Aarav on our motion notebook.

S2.text: His meter reads eighteen kilometres per hour. The road markers are in metres.

S3.text: After one second, he has gone five metres. After two seconds, ten metres.

S4.text: Let's replay the first second in slow motion. Start, and one second later, five metres.

S5.text: Five metres in every second. So eighteen kilometres per hour is five metres per second.

S6.text: Flip the unit dial. The bicycle does not change. Only the number does. Eighteen, or five.

S7.text: And on the graph, the slope is the speed. One line, written in two units.

D1.text: Now let's do it on paper, one small step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Write the unit as a fraction. Eighteen kilometres per hour is eighteen kilometres over one hour.

D3.text: Step two. Swap kilometres for metres. One kilometre is one thousand metres.

D4.text: Step three. Swap the hour for seconds. One hour is sixty times sixty, which is three thousand six hundred seconds.

D5.text: Step four. Simplify. One thousand over three thousand six hundred is five over eighteen.

D6.text: Eighteen times five over eighteen is five. Five metres per second, just like the bicycle showed.

R1.text: Now the reasoning, link by link.

R2.text: A kilometre is a big unit. In metres, the number gets bigger. That is the times one thousand.

R3.text: An hour is long. In one second, you cover much less. That is the divide by three thousand six hundred.

R4.text: Together, the number shrinks. Five over eighteen is the same as dividing by three point six.

T1.text: Remember this. Kilometres per hour to metres per second, multiply by five over eighteen. Back again, multiply by eighteen over five.

K1.text: Side by side. On the left, eighteen kilometres per hour. On the right, five metres per second.

K2.text: Same bicycle, same speed. The bigger unit always gets the smaller number.

K3.text: Now you try. A car moves at seventy-two kilometres per hour. In metres per second, is the number bigger or smaller? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Smaller! Seventy-two times five over eighteen is twenty. In one second, the car covers only twenty metres.

A1.text: Now a twist. Units with powers.

A2.text: One metre is one hundred centimetres. Easy.

A3.text: But take a square, one metre on each side. Its area is one square metre.

A4.text: In centimetres, each side is one hundred centimetres long. So how big is the area now?

A5.text: Your turn. How many square centimetres make one square metre? One hundred, or ten thousand? Pause and decide.

A6.text: Ten thousand! One hundred times one hundred. When the unit is squared, square the factor too.

A7.text: For a cube, cube it. One cubic metre is one million cubic centimetres.

W2.text: Water has a density of about one gram per cubic centimetre. What is it in kilograms per cubic metre?

W3.text: Step one. One gram is one thousandth of a kilogram. That is ten to the minus three kilograms.

W4.text: Step two. One centimetre is ten to the minus two metres. Cube it. One cubic centimetre is ten to the minus six cubic metres.

W5.text: Step three. Divide. Ten to the minus three, over ten to the minus six, is ten to the power three.

W6.text: So the density of water is about one thousand kilograms per cubic metre.

X2.text: Many students convert thirty-six kilometres per hour by multiplying by eighteen over five. They get one hundred and twenty-nine point six metres per second.

X3.text: That is backwards. In metres per second, the number must get smaller. Thirty-six times five over eighteen is ten metres per second.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As the first step inside numericals: speeds, densities, and units with powers.

Q1.text: Exam level now. g is nine point eight metres per second squared. What is it in kilometres per hour squared? Pause and solve.

A8.text: The answer is B. About one point two seven times ten to the five.

A9.text: Metres to kilometres, divide by one thousand. Per second squared to per hour squared, multiply by three thousand six hundred, squared.

A10.text: Option A forgot to square. Option C forgot the thousand. Option D turned the factor upside down.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is eighteen kilometres per hour not eighteen metres per second?

Y3.text: Two. What is fifty-four kilometres per hour in metres per second?

Y4.text: Three. How many cubic centimetres make one cubic metre, and why?

N1.text: Next time: can you add five metres to five seconds? We find out in dimensions of physical quantities.
